knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, error = FALSE,
                      out.width = if (knitr::is_html_output()) "100%" else "6.5in")
library(data.table)

# chunk, so that the two documents never disagree, and then reads what the paper has no space for
paper_lines <- readLines(resrepo::path_resrepo("writing/paper_draft.Rmd"), encoding = "UTF-8")
s <- grep("^```\\{r setup", paper_lines)

# --- Results kept from the earlier working document (s03, s04, s05, s11, s12, s13, s14) ---
d3 <- dir_int("s03_explore_climate")
d4 <- dir_int("s04_fit_phylogenetic_models")
d17 <- dir_int("s17_make_figures")
checks <- read(d3, "realm_transfer_checks_500km.csv")
ck <- function(rg, col) checks[held_out == rg][[col]]
cv <- read(d4, "lineage_cv_species.csv")
cv_med <- function(ct, sch) median(cv[contrast == ct & scheme == sch]$cv_d2)
imp <- read(d4, "lineage_cv_importance.csv")
im <- function(v, col) imp[contrast == "obligate" & variable == v][[col]]
het <- read(d5, "region_heterogeneity_species.csv")
hp <- function(ct, v) het[contrast == ct & variable == v]$p
cons <- read(d5, "region_slope_consistency.csv")
sef12_t <- read(d12, "stability_evidence_effects.csv")
sef12 <- function(ev, an, col = "estimate") sef12_t[evidence == ev & analysis == an][[col]]
snl <- read(d14, "seasonality_null.csv")
snp <- function(ct) snl[contrast == ct, mean(estimate >= estimate[permutation == 0])]
shq <- function(a, v, q) quantile(shn[permutation > 0 & area == a & variable == v]$within_lineage, q)
sphy <- read(d11, "seasonality_phylo.csv")
sp11 <- function(tr, ct, col = "estimate") sphy[tree == tr & contrast == ct][[col]]
stran <- read(d11, "subfamily_transfer.csv")
mixg <- read(d11, "mixed_genera.csv")
mixg[, obligate := mutualist + parasite]
sreg <- read(d13, "species_region_effects.csv")

# --- Dry-niche test (s36) ---
pil36 <- read(d36, "pilot_estimates.csv")
gen36 <- cg36[group == "Measure" & model == "primary" & background == "record"]
rng36 <- function(grp, bg_ = "record") range(cs36[group == grp & background == bg_]$pooled)
mp <- function(st, col = "pooled") csf(st, col = col)

# --- Confinement details (s23, s33) ---
# (version 2 of the dry-niche test, s37, is read by the paper's setup chunk: d37, jf, tsf, to37, oc37, ct37)
sc33 <- read(d33, "sister_contrasts.csv")
rmf <- function(pattern, col = "estimate") rm23[grepl(pattern, analysis)][[col]]

# --- Partner ants of obligate lycaenids (s21, s30) ---
obl_ants <- prec21[interaction_type %in% c("m", "p"),
                   .(obligate = uniqueN(pool_key),
                     mutualists = uniqueN(pool_key[interaction_type == "m"]),
                     parasites = uniqueN(pool_key[interaction_type == "p"]),
                     regions = paste(sort(unique(region)), collapse = ", ")),
                   by = .(ant_taxon, ant_genus)]
obl_ants <- merge(obl_ants, pa30[, .(ant_taxon, colony_size)], by = "ant_taxon", all.x = TRUE)
setorder(obl_ants, -obligate)
# Partner species of each region and strategy group with a colony size in the trait database
pr_cs <- merge(unique(prec21[, .(ant_taxon, region, obligate = interaction_type %in% c("m", "p"))]),
               pa30[, .(ant_taxon, colony_size)], by = "ant_taxon", all.x = TRUE)
cs_cov <- function(rg, obl) pr_cs[region == rg & obligate == obl, mean(is.finite(colony_size))]
rps <- function(rg, grp) 10^rp30[region == rg & group == grp]$median_cs
lsp <- function(col) lt30[contrast == "mutualist" & measure == "partner_cs_species" &
                            given == "region and lineage"][[col]]
```

# Climate, history and the global geography of butterfly–ant interactions {-}

**Working document: the full record of the study.** Ondrej Pelanek, with Claude (Anthropic); updated `r format(Sys.Date(), "%d %B %Y")`. The two writing files now have different jobs. The paper draft (`writing/paper_draft.Rmd`) is kept focused and paper-like, within the limits of *Global Ecology and Biogeography*. This document is comprehensive: it reports every analysis (`code/s01`–`s34`), including the details the paper has cut, and it discusses ideas, alternative explanations and projects for which the paper has no space. Both documents read the same notebook outputs through the same setup code, so their numbers always agree. Statements of pattern are kept apart from hypotheses about mechanism, which are labelled as such. The figures of each analysis are collected in Section \@ref(supplement).

## In brief {-}

1. **The strategies are structured in space and rest on few genera in each region.** Obligate associates belong to `r obligate_genera_total` genera worldwide and are concentrated in southern Africa and Australia; none of the `r lin_n("Nearctic", "n") + lin_n("Nearctic", "f") + lin_n("Neotropic", "n") + lin_n("Neotropic", "f")` classified species of the Americas is obligate. Uneven knowledge does not produce this ordering.
2. **Similar climates hold different interactions.** Within the climates the Cape shares with the Mediterranean Basin, `r pct(std(cb, "obligate_1"))` of the Cape's classified species and `r pct(std(cb, "obligate_2"))` of the Basin's are obligate associates. Compared within shared climates, southern Africa and Australia hold more obligate species than nearly every other region.
3. **Lineage predicts strategies while the genus is known; geography does better for unseen genera.** Lineage explained `r pct(oos("obligate", "all", "species held out", "lineage"))` of the held-out deviance in obligacy for species and `r pct(po("obligate", "held-out realm", "lineage"))` for whole realms, but `r pct(bg("obligate", "genus unseen", "lineage"))` for species whose genus occurs only in the held-out realm, where latitude and hemisphere explained `r pct(bg("obligate", "genus unseen", "latitude x hemisphere"))`. The climate models we tested explained at most `r pct(clim_max)`.
4. **Obligate genera are confined.** They occupy `r num(exp(-spm("Hexagons occupied (log)")), 1)` times fewer hexagons than other genera of the same age and size, under other definitions, grains and sampling controls, but less certainly when the uncertainty of classification is carried, and not clearly among sister clades (`r ss33$negative` of `r ss33$contrasts` contrasts).
5. **Obligacy has a southern geography that crosses lineages.** Glacial stability, soils, phosphorus, fire, deep-time aridity and ant richness add nothing detectable to latitude and hemisphere.
6. **Obligate mutualists live in warmer, more seasonal places than their facultative relatives, but not at matched temperature and habitat.** They use drier places than their surroundings in `r asf("mutualist", "beyond", "positive")` of `r asf("mutualist", "beyond", "genera")` mixed genera, and against a background of all butterfly records the difference is positive but uncertain (Section \@ref(dryniche)). Drought can be told apart from warmth with temperature-independent measures, yet at the same temperature the difference in dry-season length is `r ci41(p41, "H2")` SD, and within the same biome `r ci41(b41, "H2")`: a habitat difference, not a detected response to drought (Section \@ref(processes)).
7. **Ants give a mixed picture.** The main partner genera are not more prevalent where obligate lycaenids are many. Local communities are more dominated in the south, but within regions more dominated communities go with fewer obligate lycaenids. The partners of obligate lycaenids have somewhat larger colonies. Large colonies and dominant communities are different things (Section \@ref(colonies)).
8. **Obligacy may have arisen more often in the south per unit of lineage history.** The rate is `r num(min(r25$ratio_median), 1)`–`r num(max(r25$ratio_median), 1)` times that elsewhere on four trees, but with so few origins this is not clearly beyond chance.
9. **The southern faunas hold disproportionately the obligate genera of their subfamilies.** The Cape through few, entirely obligate, species-rich and narrowly distributed genera with many parasites; southern Australia through many partly obligate genera of mutualists. Both exceed a subfamily-conserving null, as do southern Africa and Australia, whereas the Mediterranean Basin does not (Section \@ref(processes)).

# Why ask this

The parent study (`butterfly_ant_interactions`) mapped the four larval strategies of lycaenids (non-associated, facultative, obligate mutualist and obligate parasite) and found them strongly structured in space. Climate, soils, aridification, glaciation, partner ants and lineage history have all been proposed to explain this geography (Pierce et al. 2002; Pierce & Dankowicz 2022), but they have not been separated. We asked how much of the geography is associated with present and past climate, and how much with the evolutionary history of the lineages that carry the strategies.

The proposed explanations act at three timescales (`writing/literature_review.md` lists twelve hypotheses):

- **present environments**, such as a cold limit on ant activity (Pellissier et al. 2012), nest refuges in seasonally dry, fire-prone biomes (Cottrell 1984; Espeland et al. 2023), or old, infertile landscapes with abundant, dominant ants (Orians & Milewski 2007; Hopper 2009);
- **Late Quaternary legacies**, such as climatic stability allowing partner-dependent specialists to persist (Dynesius & Jansson 2000; Sandel et al. 2011);
- **deep evolutionary contingency**: which lineages reached, persisted and diversified in each region (Vila et al. 2011).

Because the strategies are concentrated in few lineages, we treated lineage history as the null hypothesis that climate has to beat. Table 1 of the paper lists each explanation, its prediction, our test and the result; Section \@ref(meaning) of this document discusses what the results mean and what they do not show.

# What we did

**Data.** We used the interaction types, taxonomy and cleaned occurrence records of the companion compilation. Of the `r format(n_units, big.mark = ",")` species units with occurrence records (`r format(n_records, big.mark = ",")` unique cleaned coordinates), `r format(n_class, big.mark = ",")` were classified: `r n_type("n")` non-associated, `r n_type("f")` facultative, `r n_type("m")` obligate mutualist and `r n_type("p")` obligate parasite. Riodinidae are excluded. Assemblages were built in equal-area squares of 250, 500 and 1,000 km (the 500-km cells are identical to the parent study's Fig. 1) and in ISEA hexagons of about 23,000 to 630,000 km². Each species was described by the median over the 10-arc-minute pixels holding its records. The layers covered present climate (WorldClim 2.1, with Hargreaves aridity, dry months and water-deficit months), the temperature and precipitation change since the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) and its velocity, soils (SoilGrids 2.0 and phosphorus), fire (GFED5), 5-Myr precipitation (PALEO-PGEM), land cover (EarthEnv consensus), net primary productivity and elevation. For ants we used estimated richness (Kass et al. 2022), partner records, local communities (Global Ant Database; Gibb et al. 2017) and colony traits (Bell-Roberts et al. 2024).

**Approach.** We asked the question in five ways, each designed so that lineage history could explain the result without climate:

1. **Across regions**, we compared regions within the climates they share (Section \@ref(shared)).
2. **Among species**, we compared climate and lineage as predictors of species, genera, subfamilies and realms left out of the fit (Section \@ref(lineage)).
3. **Within regions**, we compared the composition of each cell with that expected from the genera present (Section \@ref(within)).
4. **Among genera**, we related the spread of genera to obligacy (Section \@ref(confinement)).
5. **Given region and lineage**, we tested what environmental and ant variables still go with obligacy (Sections \@ref(southern) and \@ref(ants)), and how often obligacy arose in each region (Section \@ref(history)).

**The notebooks.** Each analysis is one notebook in `code/`, run in order by `code/run_all.R`:

| Notebook | Question |
|---|---|
| s01–s02 | Climate layers; species-by-cell assemblages and species climates |
| s03–s04 | Exploratory cell models; species-level climate and lineage, phylogenetic logistic regression |
| s05 | Strategies within the eight biogeographic regions; composition along gradients against the lineages present |
| s06, s08 | Glacial stability or southern geography; soils, fire and drought beyond latitude and hemisphere |
| s07, s13, s18, s24 | Mediterranean-climate regions; comparisons within shared climate strata, their audit, and every pair of regions |
| s09, s10, s14, s25 | Origins of obligacy on four trees; matched-only trees; rates of origin per unit of lineage history |
| s11, s19, s28, s29, s31, s32, s34 | Seasonality and drought given region and lineage, within genera; robustness; availability; habitat; flight; accessible areas |
| s35, s36 | The dry-niche test: an all-butterfly background, accessible areas defined in advance, presence–background models, one estimate per genus |
| s12, s26 | Evidence and knowledge: species-specific evidence, imputation, sampling |
| s15 | Ant association along latitude in Europe, the eastern Palaearctic and the Nearctic |
| s16, s17, s22 | Maps and figures |
| s20 | Prediction of held-out realms and subfamilies; known and unseen genera |

| s23, s33 | Spread of genera and its robustness |

# Findings

## The strategies are structured in space and rest on few genera {#structure}

```{r fig-world, fig.cap = "Global distribution of the ant-interaction strategies, in ISEA hexagons of about 210,000 km² (Equal Earth projection). (a–d) Proportions of classified species that were non-associated, facultative, obligate mutualists and obligate parasites, in hexagons with at least ten classified species; each panel has its own square-root colour scale, spanning the 1st to 99th percentiles of its hexagons. (e) Classified species per hexagon. (f) Share of the recorded species of each hexagon that is classified. Grey land has no estimate."}
fig(d16, "plot_world_strategies.png")
```

Obligate mutualists are concentrated in southern Africa and Australia, obligate parasites in southern Africa, and non-associated species in the Holarctic, especially in North America and the far east of Asia (Fig. \@ref(fig:fig-world)). The regions differ less in how many of their species are associated with ants, from `r pct(min(assoc_share$share))` in the `r assoc_share$region[which.min(assoc_share$share)]` to `r pct(max(assoc_share$share))` in `r south(assoc_share$region[which.max(assoc_share$share)])`, than in how they are associated:

- southern Africa holds `r lin_n("Southern Africa", "p")` obligate parasites in only `r lin_n("Southern Africa", "p", "genera")` genera and `r lin_n("Southern Africa", "m")` obligate mutualists in `r lin_n("Southern Africa", "m", "genera")` genera;
- Australia holds `r lin_n("Australia", "m")` obligate mutualists in `r lin_n("Australia", "m", "genera")` genera;
- the Palaearctic has `r lin_n("Palearctic", "p")` parasites in `r lin_n("Palearctic", "p", "genera")` genera, and the Americas none.

Any regional relationship between climate and the obligate strategies therefore rests on a handful of lineages.

**Uneven knowledge does not produce the ordering.** Classification is uneven: `r pct(ecomp("Australia"))` of the recorded species of Australia and `r pct(ecomp("Southern Africa"))` of southern Africa are classified, against `r pct(ecomp("Tropical Africa"))` of tropical Africa, `r pct(ecomp("Neotropic"))` of the Neotropics and `r pct(ecomp("New Guinea and islands"))` of New Guinea. The sources also often give a type for a genus or for relatives rather than for the species itself: `r pct(epres("p"))` of the obligate parasites, `r pct(epres("f"))` of the facultative species, `r pct(epres("n"))` of the non-associated species and `r pct(epres("m"))` of the obligate mutualists. We checked this in three ways (`s26`):

- with species-specific evidence only, obligate associates made up `r pct(kr("Southern Africa", "Species-specific evidence only"))` of the species of southern Africa and `r pct(kr("Australia", "Species-specific evidence only"))` of Australia, against at most `r pct(max(kspec[!region %in% c("Southern Africa", "Australia")]$obligate_share))` elsewhere;
- imputing unclassified species from their congeners changed no region but `r south(kimp[which.min(change)]$region)` by more than `r pts(max(abs(kimp[-which.min(change)]$change)))` points (tropical Africa fell from `r pct(kr("Tropical Africa", "All classified species"))` to `r pct(kr("Tropical Africa", "Unclassified species imputed from relatives"))`, because its unclassified species belong mostly to facultative genera);
- obligate species had `r pct(1 - 10^smp26$estimate)` fewer GBIF records than facultative species of the same region and lineage (`r pval(smp26$p)`), so if anything they are under-recorded, not over-studied.

The upper bounds tell the other side of the story: if every unclassified species were obligate, the obligate share could reach `r pct(kr("Neotropic", "All classified species", "upper_bound"))` in the Neotropics and `r pct(kr("Indomalayan", "All classified species", "upper_bound"))` in Indomalaya. Nothing suggests that it does, but the Neotropics remain the least known fauna.

## Similar climates hold different interactions {#shared}

```{r fig-shared, fig.cap = "Similar climates, different interactions (Figure 2 of the paper). (a) Hexagons of about 70,000 km² with land in the climate strata of the Mediterranean-climate parts of the Cape or southern Australia, coloured by the obligate share of each region in these climates. (b) Share of each strategy in the Cape or southern Australia (filled) and the Mediterranean Basin (open) within the strata each pair shares, standardised to a common distribution over the strata, with 95% intervals from resampling genera. (c) The difference under every variant of the comparison. (d) Southern Africa or Australia against each other region within the strata they share across all their land; grey band: range among the pairs of other regions."}
fig(d22, "figure_2_shared_climates.png")
```

If climate shaped the strategies, regions with the same climate should hold similar strategy mixes. We tested this in four steps.

**First, the five Mediterranean-climate regions hold five different faunas.** Obligate associates make up `r pct(mob("Cape"))` of the `r mn("Cape")` classified species of the Cape and `r pct(mob("Southern Australia"))` of the `r mn("Southern Australia")` of southern Australia, against `r pct(mob("Mediterranean Basin"))` of the `r mn("Mediterranean Basin")` of the Mediterranean Basin and none of the `r mn("California")` of California or the `r mn("Central Chile")` of central Chile.

**Second, the difference holds within the climates the regions share** (Fig. \@ref(fig:fig-shared)b, c). Within the `r std(cb, "strata")` strata shared by the Cape and the Basin, standardised to the same distribution over the strata, `r pct(std(cb, "obligate_1"))` of the Cape's species and `r pct(std(cb, "obligate_2"))` of the Basin's were obligate (difference `r pts(std(cb, "difference"))` points, 95% interval `r pts(std(cb, "difference_low"))`–`r pts(std(cb, "difference_high"))`). Both obligate strategies contributed: mutualists made up `r pct(sh18(cb, "Cape", "m"))` against `r pct(sh18(cb, "Mediterranean Basin", "m"))`, and parasites `r pct(sh18(cb, "Cape", "p"))` against `r pct(sh18(cb, "Mediterranean Basin", "p"))`. The contrast held under every variant:

- `r pts(std(cb, "difference", wt = "equal weights"))` points with equal stratum weights;
- `r pts(std(cb, "difference", ver = "main stratum of each species"))` points when each species counted only in its main stratum;
- `r pts(ssp(cb, "difference"))` points with species-specific evidence only;
- `r pts(min(sens18[pair == cb]$difference))`–`r pts(max(sens18[pair == cb]$difference))` points for every stratum width (half to twice as wide) and minimum occupancy (one to ten pixels), with lower bounds of at least `r pts(min(sens18[pair == cb]$difference_low))` points;
- `r pts(std(cb, "difference", ver = "genus-weighted"))` points (`r pts(std(cb, "difference_low", ver = "genus-weighted"))`–`r pts(std(cb, "difference_high", ver = "genus-weighted"))`) when each genus counted once per region and stratum.

Southern Australia differed from the Basin by `r pts(std(ab, "difference"))` points (`r pts(std(ab, "difference_low"))`–`r pts(std(ab, "difference_high"))`), a difference of similar size in every variant but with lower bounds close to zero.

**What the matching retains.** Matching balanced the climates of the Cape and the Basin (standardised mean differences of temperature, aridity and seasonality at most `r num(max(abs(bal18[pair == cb & variable != "bio06"]$smd_after)))` after weighting, from up to `r num(max(abs(bal18[pair == cb & variable != "bio06"]$smd_before)))`; minimum temperature remained higher in the Cape). But it covered only `r pct(rt(cb, "Mediterranean Basin", "share_pixels"))` of the Basin's Mediterranean-climate pixels and `r pct(rt(cb, "Mediterranean Basin", "share_species"))` of its classified species, against `r pct(rt(cb, "Cape", "share_pixels"))` and `r pct(rt(cb, "Cape", "share_species"))` of the Cape's. The comparison is therefore one of the Cape against the warm, dry, frost-free margin of the Basin, which is where the Basin is most like the Cape; it is not a comparison of the two faunas as wholes. California shares no stratum with the Cape or southern Australia, so it is not a climatic replicate of the southern regions.

**Species richness or genus richness?** The two southern regions reach their obligate richness differently. Decomposing the difference from the Basin into a part due to holding more obligate genera and a part due to the richness of those genera, the genus part accounted for `r pct(dc("Cape", "Mediterranean Basin", "G_share_of_S"))` of the Cape's excess and `r pct(dc("Southern Australia", "Mediterranean Basin", "G_share_of_S"))` of southern Australia's. In the Cape the three largest obligate genera hold `r pct(gwv("Cape", "top3_obligate_share"))` of its obligate species; southern Australia has many obligate genera with few species each. With genus weights, the Cape and southern Australia did not differ (`r pts(std("Cape vs Southern Australia", "difference", ver = "genus-weighted"))` points).

**Third, the lineages differ.** None of the obligate species of the Cape or southern Australia belongs to a genus that also occurs in the Basin or California; the genera they share (for example *Leptotes*, *Lampides*, *Zizeeria* and *Lycaena*) are represented only by facultative or non-associated species there. Given each species' own climate, the species of the Cape and southern Australia remained far more often obligate than those of the Basin (log odds `r num(sreg[model == "Region + species climate" & region == "Cape"]$estimate, 1)` and `r num(sreg[model == "Region + species climate" & region == "Southern Australia"]$estimate, 1)`).

**Fourth, the southern excess is general** (Fig. \@ref(fig:fig-shared)d). Within the climate strata they share across all their land, southern Africa held more obligate species than `r aps("Southern Africa vs other regions", "intervals_above_zero")` of the `r aps("Southern Africa vs other regions", "pairs")` other regions with at least five shared strata, and Australia than `r aps("Australia vs other regions", "intervals_above_zero")` of `r aps("Australia vs other regions", "pairs")`, by medians of `r pts(aps("Southern Africa vs other regions", "median_difference"))` and `r pts(aps("Australia vs other regions", "median_difference"))` points; the intervals included zero only for `r ap_ns`. The two did not differ from each other (`r pts(ap24[pair == "Southern Africa vs Australia"]$difference)` points). The `r aps("Control pairs", "pairs")` pairs of the other regions differed by a median of `r pts(aps("Control pairs", "median_abs_difference"))` points; the largest differences separated the Neotropics, which hold no obligate species, from Indomalaya and New Guinea.

**The Americas lack the obligate associates their climates predict.** Climate models fitted to all other realms predicted that `r pct(ck("Nearctic", "obligate_predicted_inside"))` of the associated species in Nearctic cells would be obligate, in the `r pct(ck("Nearctic", "share_cells_inside_training_range"))` of cells whose climates lie inside the range of the training realms; none is (Table \@ref(tab:tab-americas)). The Nearctic fauna is well classified (median coverage `r pct(ck("Nearctic", "median_coverage"))` per cell), so incomplete data cannot explain the absence there.

```{r tab-americas}
tab <- checks[, .(`Held-out realm` = held_out, Cells = cells,
                  `Median coverage` = pct(median_coverage),
                  `Cells inside training climate` = pct(share_cells_inside_training_range),
                  `Obligate share observed (inside)` = pct(obligate_observed_inside),
                  `Obligate share predicted (inside)` = pct(obligate_predicted_inside))]
knitr::kable(tab, caption = "Transfer of climate-only cell models (500-km cells, s03) to each held-out realm: classification coverage, the share of cells with every predictor inside the range of the training realms, and the observed and predicted obligate share of associated species in those cells.")
```

## Lineage predicts strategies while the genus is known {#lineage}

```{r fig-lineage, fig.cap = "Lineage and climate as predictors of obligacy, and the spread of obligate genera (Figure 3 of the paper). (a) Observed and predicted obligate share of each held-out realm. (b) Hexagons occupied by obligate and other genera, adjusted to the mean stem age and recorded species. (c) Deviance explained for the obligacy of held-out species, genera, realms (split into known and new genera) and subfamilies by lineage, climate and latitude with hemisphere."}
fig(d22, "figure_3_lineage_climate.png")
```

**In sample, lineage describes most of the variation.** Subfamily and genus described `r pct(ps("associated", "lineage"))` of the deviance in ant association, `r pct(ps("obligate", "lineage"))` in obligacy and `r pct(ps("parasite", "lineage"))` in parasitism against mutualism; climate described `r pct(ps("associated", "climate"))`, `r pct(ps("obligate", "climate"))` and `r pct(ps("parasite", "climate"))`, almost all of it shared with lineage. Only `r ps("obligate", "mixed_genera")` genera contain both obligate and facultative species, and `r ps("parasite", "mixed_genera")` both parasites and mutualists. In-sample shares measure description, not generality, so we judged the models on held-out units.

**Held-out species and genera.** For species held out of the fit, lineage explained `r pct(oos("associated", "all", "species held out", "lineage"))`, `r pct(oos("obligate", "all", "species held out", "lineage"))` and `r pct(oos("parasite", "all", "species held out", "lineage"))` of the deviance in the three contrasts, and climate at most `r pct(max(oos_t[scheme == "species held out" & model == "climate" & evidence == "all"]$d2))`. With species-specific evidence only, lineage still explained `r pct(oos("associated", "specific", "species held out", "lineage"))`, `r pct(oos("obligate", "specific", "species held out", "lineage"))` and `r pct(oos("parasite", "specific", "species held out", "lineage"))`, so the types presumed from relatives inflate the lineage signal only slightly. For held-out genera, of which the model knew only the subfamily, lineage explained `r pct(oos("associated", "all", "genera held out", "lineage"))`, `r pct(oos("obligate", "all", "genera held out", "lineage"))` and `r pct(oos("parasite", "all", "genera held out", "lineage"))`: the subfamily predicts association but not obligacy, because obligate and facultative genera are mixed within subfamilies.

**Held-out realms.** When each realm was predicted from the other seven, lineage explained `r pct(po("obligate", "held-out realm", "lineage"))` of the deviance in obligacy (`r pct(po("obligate", "held-out realm", "lineage", "d2_low"))`–`r pct(po("obligate", "held-out realm", "lineage", "d2_high"))`; AUC `r num(po("obligate", "held-out realm", "lineage", "auc"))`), latitude and hemisphere `r pct(po("obligate", "held-out realm", "latitude x hemisphere"))` and climate `r pct(po("obligate", "held-out realm", "climate"))`. Climate forecast `r pct(me("obligate", "held-out realm", "Neotropic", "climate"))` obligate species among the associated species of the Neotropics and `r pct(me("obligate", "held-out realm", "Palearctic", "climate"))` of the Palaearctic, against `r pct(me("obligate", "held-out realm", "Neotropic", "climate", "observed"))` and `r pct(me("obligate", "held-out realm", "Palearctic", "climate", "observed"))` observed, and `r pct(me("obligate", "held-out realm", "Southern Africa", "climate"))` for southern Africa, against `r pct(me("obligate", "held-out realm", "Southern Africa", "climate", "observed"))`. These were not extrapolations: at most `r pct(novel_max)` of the species of any held-out realm lay outside the climates of the training species. Flexible climate models (smooth terms with a temperature–aridity interaction) did no better (`r pct(fc("obligate", "held-out realm", "climate (flexible)"))` for realms, `r pct(fc("obligate", "held-out subfamily", "climate (flexible)"))` for subfamilies).

**Known and new genera.** The lineage model's advantage in held-out realms came from genera shared between realms. It explained `r pct(bg("obligate", "genus known", "lineage"))` of the deviance for the `r bg("obligate", "genus known", "lineage", "species")` species whose genus also occurred in the training realms (AUC `r num(bg("obligate", "genus known", "lineage", "auc"))`), but `r pct(bg("obligate", "genus unseen", "lineage"))` for the `r bg("obligate", "genus unseen", "lineage", "species")` species of genera found only in the held-out realm. For those, latitude and hemisphere explained `r pct(bg("obligate", "genus unseen", "latitude x hemisphere"))` and climate `r pct(bg("obligate", "genus unseen", "climate"))`. Lineage thus predicted Australia poorly (`r pct(me("obligate", "held-out realm", "Australia", "lineage"))` against `r pct(me("obligate", "held-out realm", "Australia", "lineage", "observed"))` observed), because its obligate genera are endemic, whereas latitude and hemisphere predicted `r pct(me("obligate", "held-out realm", "Australia", "latitude x hemisphere"))`. This is the sharpest statement of the study's two halves: lineage carries the strategies where lineages are shared, and something geographic, not captured by the climate variables, marks the regions where new obligate lineages appear.

**Held-out subfamilies.** For obligacy alone, geography and climate predicted subfamilies the model had not seen (latitude and hemisphere `r pct(po("obligate", "held-out subfamily", "latitude x hemisphere"))`, climate `r pct(po("obligate", "held-out subfamily", "climate"))`, lineage `r pct(po("obligate", "held-out subfamily", "lineage"))`). In the earlier cross-validation (`s04`), the climate signal for subfamilies came mainly from the LGM temperature anomaly: alone it predicted held-out subfamilies with D² = `r num(im("lgm_anomaly_temperature", "cv_d2_alone"))`, and dropping it from the six predictors lost `r num(im("lgm_anomaly_temperature", "cv_d2_loss_when_dropped"))`. Section \@ref(southern) shows that this is southern geography rather than demonstrably glacial stability. Climate did not predict the association (`r num(cv_med("associated", "subfamily"))`) or parasitism (`r num(cv_med("parasite", "subfamily"))`) of held-out subfamilies.

## Within regions, climate gradients are mostly lineage turnover {#within}

```{r fig-europe, fig.cap = "Ant association along latitude in Europe (s15). (A) Share of non-associated species among the classified species of hexagons of about 23,000 km². (B) Mean species richness per hexagon of non-associated, facultative and obligate species in 3° latitude bands. (C) Non-associated share along latitude, observed and expected from the genera present. (D) Species per hexagon of each genus in the north (above 56° N) relative to the south (below 46° N)."}
fig(d15, "plot_europe_association.png")
```

Within regions, composition changes along climate gradients: in the Palaearctic and Nearctic, non-associated species become more frequent towards cold and wet climates; in Australia, facultative associates increase and obligate mutualists decrease towards warm climates; in southern Africa, obligate mutualists increase towards dry climates. Such a gradient can arise because the genera present change along it or because species of the same genera change strategy along it. We gave each species the strategy composition of its congeners (itself excluded) and compared the composition expected from the genera present with the observed one.

- **The genera present reproduce most gradients.** Of the `r nrow(gb)` regional gradients steeper than 0.3 log odds per SD, the lineage expectation had the same sign in `r pct(mean(sign(gb$expected_slope) == sign(gb$observed_slope)))` and reproduced a median `r pct(median(gb$expected_slope / gb$observed_slope))` of the observed slope; `r pct(mean(cons$same_sign >= 0.9))` of the relationships kept their sign in at least 90% of alternative grids, grains, weightings and minimum numbers of species.
- **Strategies shift little within genera.** Against permutations of strategies among the species of each genus, the part not reproduced by lineages was larger than chance on average (mean z = `r num(gnt$mean_z_observed)`, `r pval(gnt$p_one_sided)`), but exceeded the permutation range in only `r gnt$slopes_beyond_null` of the `r gnt$slopes` gradients.
- **Europe shows how this works.** The share of non-associated species rises northwards. Per 10° of latitude, facultative richness per hexagon fell by `r pct(-rs("Europe", "facultative_change_per_10deg"))`, while non-associated richness did not change (`r pct(rs("Europe", "non_associated_change_per_10deg"), 1)`). The share expected from the genera present rose almost as steeply as the observed one (`r num(shv("Europe", "latitude_z", "expected_slope"))` against `r num(shv("Europe", "latitude_z", "observed_slope"))` log odds per SD), and the remainder (`r num(shv("Europe", "latitude_z", "within_lineage"))`) was within the within-genus permutations (`r num(shq("Europe", "latitude_z", 0.025))` to `r num(shq("Europe", "latitude_z", 0.975))`). *Lysandra*, *Leptotes*, *Lampides*, *Tomares*, *Kretania* and *Iolana* thin sharply northwards, and *Polyommatus* falls from `r num(eug[genus == "Polyommatus"]$south, 1)` species per hexagon in the south to `r num(eug[genus == "Polyommatus"]$north, 1)` in the north, while *Lycaena*, *Callophrys* and *Agriades* persist. The trend is a loss of the southern facultative radiations, not of facultative association as such. Latitude and temperature are too closely correlated in Europe (r = `r num(smd[area == "Europe"]$correlation_latitude_temperature[1])`) to be separated.
- **The pattern is European.** In the Nearctic the non-associated share hardly changed with latitude (deviance explained `r pct(sm("Nearctic", "latitude"), 1)`), and in the eastern Palaearctic non-associated richness fell faster than facultative richness.
- **Among species, temperature does not predict association within regions.** Given lineage, the effect of a species' temperature on association was weak in the Palaearctic (`r num(aef[region == "Palearctic" & model == "Given lineage"]$estimate)`, `r pval(aef[region == "Palearctic" & model == "Given lineage"]$p)`) and the Nearctic (`r num(aef[region == "Nearctic" & model == "Given lineage"]$estimate)`), and positive only in Indomalaya (`r num(aef[region == "Indomalayan" & model == "Given lineage"]$estimate)`), not within genera there. The relationships also differed among regions (`r pval(hp("associated", "bio01"))` for temperature). This sits uneasily with the Alpine result of Pellissier et al. (2012), in which species with weaker ant interactions occur in colder places; at continental scale, the same pattern arises mainly from which genera reach the cold.

## Obligate genera are confined {#confinement}

The idea behind this test is that dependence on particular ants may limit how far a lineage spreads. If so, obligate genera should occupy fewer places than other genera of the same age and richness.

**The main result.** At a given stem age and number of recorded species, obligate genera (at least half of their classified species obligate) occupied `r num(exp(-spm("Hexagons occupied (log)")), 1)` times fewer hexagons of about 210,000 km² (`r pval(spm("Hexagons occupied (log)", "p"))`; Fig. \@ref(fig:fig-lineage)b), `r num(exp(-spm("Hexagons occupied (log), phylogenetic")), 1)` times fewer in phylogenetic regression on the tree of genera (`r pval(spm("Hexagons occupied (log), phylogenetic", "p"))`), and reached fewer regions beyond the first (`r pval(spm("Regions beyond the first (Poisson)", "p"))`), although they were not detectably more often confined to a single region (`r pval(spm("Confined to one region (logistic)", "p"))`). Of the `r nrow(ogr23)` obligate genera recorded in more than one region, `r ogr23[regions == 2, .N]` occurred in only two, such as *Lepidochrysops* in southern and tropical Africa and *Hypochrysops* in Australia and New Guinea.

**Robustness (`s33`).** The association held, at `r num(min(cr33_main$ratio), 1)`–`r num(max(cr33_main$ratio), 1)` times fewer hexagons (all p ≤ `r num(max(cr33_main$p), 3)`), under every variant that keeps all genera:

- other definitions of an obligate genus: any obligate species (`r num(crf("Any obligate species"), 1)` times), three quarters (`r num(crf("At least three quarters obligate"), 1)`), all (`r num(crf("All classified species obligate"), 1)`), and the obligate share as a continuous variable (`r num(crf("Obligate share (continuous)"), 1)`, an entirely obligate against an entirely facultative genus);
- genera at least half or three quarters classified (`r num(crf("Genera at least 50% classified"), 1)` and `r num(crf("Genera at least 75% classified"), 1)` times, with only `r crf("Genera at least 75% classified", "genera")` genera in the latter);
- hexagons three times finer or coarser;
- given the log occurrence records of each genus (`r num(crf("With log occurrence records of the genus"), 1)` times), so obligate genera are not merely less recorded;
- given subfamily (`r num(crf("With subfamily"), 1)`) or the spread of the rest of the subfamily (`r num(crf("With the spread of the rest of the subfamily"), 1)`).

**Where it weakens.** It was weaker within Theclinae (`r num(crf("Within Theclinae"), 1)` times, `r pval(crf("Within Theclinae", "p"))`; `r crf("Within Theclinae", "genera")` genera) and not detectable within Aphnaeinae (`r crf("Within Aphnaeinae", "genera")` genera, of which `r crf("Within Aphnaeinae", "obligate_genera")` obligate). When each genus's obligate share was redrawn from its classified species, to carry the uncertainty of incomplete classification, the estimate stayed at `r num(crf("Obligate share, redrawn for incomplete classification"), 1)` times but became uncertain (`r pval(crf("Obligate share, redrawn for incomplete classification", "p"))`). Among close relatives it was not clear: in `r ss33$negative` of `r ss33$contrasts` contrasts with their sister clades on the tree of genera, obligate genera occupied fewer places than expected from their age and richness (sign test `r pval(ss33$sign_test_p)`). The largest deficits were those of *Lepidochrysops* against *Euchrysops* (`r num(sc33[genus == "Lepidochrysops"]$hexagons, 0)` against `r num(sc33[genus == "Lepidochrysops"]$sister_hexagons, 0)` hexagons) and *Thestor* against *Lachnocnema*; *Hypochrysops*, *Phengaris* and *Liphyra* occupied more places than their sister clades.

**Species ranges.** Among associated species, obligate species had smaller ranges than facultative species of the same region and lineage (coefficient `r num(rmf("^All associated"))`, `r pval(rmf("^All associated", "p"))`), but not within the genera that contain both (`r num(rmf("^Within mixed"))`, `r pval(rmf("^Within mixed", "p"))`; `r rmf("^Within mixed", "species")` species). This matters for interpretation (Section \@ref(confined)): a direct effect of dependence on spread predicts smaller ranges for obligate species also among congeners.

## A southern geography of obligacy {#southern}

```{r fig-remaining, fig.cap = "What remains once region and lineage are known (Figure 4 of the paper). (a) Deviance explained for the obligacy of held-out subfamilies by geography, geography with one property added, and each property alone. (b) For every origin of obligate mutualism, mutualists minus facultative relatives in the run of months below 50 mm, unmatched, at the same temperature, and at the same temperature and biome (s41). (c) The pooled estimates for warmth, dry-season length and water stress at each level of matching."}
fig(d22, "figure_4_remaining_signal.png")
```

**Glacial stability or southern geography? (`s06`, `s12`).** Latitude and hemisphere predicted the obligacy of held-out subfamilies (D² = `r num(sc("latitude x hemisphere", "subfamily"))`) better than the LGM temperature anomaly (`r num(sc("anomaly", "subfamily"))`), and adding the anomaly did not improve them (`r num(sc("latitude x hemisphere + anomaly", "subfamily"))`). Given region and lineage, the anomaly had no detectable effect (`r num(se("All associated species"))` log odds per SD, `r pval(se("All associated species", "p"))`), in each hemisphere, without southern Africa, without *Lepidochrysops*, *Thestor* or *Chrysoritis*, within genera, with a second reconstruction (Beyer et al. 2020) and with species-specific evidence only (`r num(sef12("specific", "Given region and lineage"))`, `r pval(sef12("specific", "Given region and lineage", "p"))`). The test is weak: its 95% interval (`r num(se("All associated species") - 1.96 * se("All associated species", "se"))` to `r num(se("All associated species") + 1.96 * se("All associated species", "se"))`) leaves effects of up to `r num(exp(1.96 * se("All associated species", "se") + abs(se("All associated species"))), 1)`-fold odds per SD compatible with the data. Glacial stability is therefore not excluded; it is not separable from whatever else distinguishes the southern continents. Two further checks (`s01`): the reconstruction has no climate under the LGM ice, so glaciated cells were filled from the nearest ice-free land; and its 800-kyr variability is the same quantity as the LGM anomaly (r = 0.99), so it is not a separate test.

**Soils, fire and deep-time aridity (`s08`).** Added to latitude and hemisphere, no soil property (including phosphorus), burned fraction, aridity or 5-Myr precipitation raised the deviance explained in held-out subfamilies by more than `r num(100 * max(dgain[scheme == "subfamily"]$gain), 1)` percentage points. Given region and lineage, none survived Holm adjustment (adjusted p ≥ `r num(min(holm19[property %in% c("phh2o", "cec", "nitrogen", "soc", "soil_p", "fire", "pgem_log_precipitation", "pgem_dry_share", "log_aridity")]$p_holm))`). These tests do not address the hypothesis of old, infertile landscapes as a history: present soils measured at 0–30 cm are a weak proxy for the long-term nutrient regime of a landscape.

**Seasonal rainfall and dry months (`s11`, `s19`).** Given region and lineage, obligate associates lived in more seasonal climates (`r num(se11("obligate", "Reference: region and lineage"))` log odds per SD, `r pval(se11("obligate", "Reference: region and lineage", "p"))`), also with species-specific evidence only, without the three largest southern obligate genera, within genera (permutation p = `r num(snp("obligate"), 3)` among the species of each genus), and in phylogenetic logistic regression with region (Schär tree `r pval(sp11("schar_2018", "obligate", "p"))`; Yumnam tree `r pval(sp11("yumnam_2025", "obligate", "p"))`). Because seasonality measures how uneven rainfall is, not how long the dry season lasts, we added dry months, the longest dry spell and driest-month precipitation (`s19`). Dry months had the largest effect (`r num(dr("obligate", "dry_months"))` log odds per SD, `r pval(dr("obligate", "dry_months", "p"))`; obligate mutualists `r num(dr("mutualist", "dry_months"))`), and after Holm adjustment over `r nrow(holm19)` properties only dry months remained below 0.05, narrowly (`r pval(hb("dry_months", "p_holm"))`). Parasites did not differ from mutualists in any of these properties. The association was regional: within single regions it was positive in Australia (`r num(se11("obligate", "Within Australia"))`) and Indomalaya (`r num(se11("obligate", "Within Indomalayan"))`), near zero in the Palaearctic and negative in southern Africa (`r num(se11("obligate", "Within Southern Africa"))`, `r pval(se11("obligate", "Within Southern Africa", "p"))`). It did not predict new lineages: adding seasonality to latitude and hemisphere changed the deviance explained in held-out subfamilies by at most `r num(100 * max(abs(stran[set == "latitude x hemisphere + seasonality"]$d2 - stran[set == "latitude x hemisphere"]$d2)), 0)` percentage points.

**Few genera carry it (`s19`, `s28`).** Within the `r nrow(mix19)` genera with both obligate and facultative species, obligate species lived in climates with more dry months than their congeners (conditional logistic regression `r num(wg("obligate", "dry_months", "conditional_estimate"))`, `r pval(wg("obligate", "dry_months", "conditional_p"))`). But the signal rests on mostly Australian and Indomalayan Theclinae (*Hypochrysops*, *Arhopala*, *Ogyris*): leaving out *Arhopala* alone weakened the effect given region and lineage to `r num(logo28[left_out == "Arhopala" & analysis == "Given region and lineage"]$estimate)` (`r pval(logo28[left_out == "Arhopala" & analysis == "Given region and lineage"]$p)`), and weighting every mixed genus equally gave `r gb28$positive` of `r gb28$genera` genera in the expected direction (sign test `r pval(gb28$sign_test_p)`). Months of water deficit showed no association given region and lineage (`r pval(drb("obligate", "deficit_months", "Given region and lineage", "p"))`), although they did in phylogenetic logistic regressions. Of the parasites with a recorded diet, `r carn19[strategy == "p"]$carnivorous` of `r carn19[strategy == "p"]$carnivory_recorded` are carnivorous in ant nests, against `r carn19[strategy == "m"]$carnivorous` of `r carn19[strategy == "m"]$carnivory_recorded` mutualists, so the association concerns larvae tended by ants rather than those that prey on them.

**Dry months available and used (`s29`).** We split each species' dry months into those available (the mean over all land in the hexagons holding its records) and its use beyond them. Given region and lineage, with both in one model, use beyond availability went with obligate mutualism (`r num(avf("mutualist", "beyond", mo = "together"))`, `r pval(avf("mutualist", "beyond", "p", mo = "together"))`) more clearly than availability (`r num(avf("mutualist", "available", mo = "together"))`, `r pval(avf("mutualist", "available", "p", mo = "together"))`). Within the mixed genera the split was sharper: the mutualists used drier places than their facultative congeners in `r asf("mutualist", "beyond", "positive")` of `r asf("mutualist", "beyond", "genera")` genera (`r pval(asf("mutualist", "beyond", "sign_test_p"))`; conditional estimate `r num(awf("mutualist", "beyond"))`, `r pval(awf("mutualist", "beyond", "p"))`), whereas their available dry months were higher in only `r asf("mutualist", "available", "positive")` (`r num(awf("mutualist", "available"))`, `r pval(awf("mutualist", "available", "p"))`). With hexagons three times larger, availability contributed as well (`r num(awf("mutualist", "available", gr = "hex4"))`, `r pval(awf("mutualist", "available", "p", gr = "hex4"))`). The raw dry months themselves were higher in the mutualists in only `r asf("mutualist", "used", "positive")` of `r asf("mutualist", "used", "genera")` genera: the consistency appears only once the surroundings are taken out.

**What the drier places are (`s31`).** Within genera, the mutualists' places had less rain in the driest month than their surroundings (`r num(hef(wg_, "Alone: Driest-month precipitation (log)", "log_bio14"))`, `r pval(hef(wg_, "Alone: Driest-month precipitation (log)", "log_bio14", "p"))`) and less shrub cover (`r num(hef(wg_, "Alone: Shrub cover", "shrub"))`, `r pval(hef(wg_, "Alone: Shrub cover", "shrub", "p"))`), and were warmer (`r num(hef(wg_, "Alone: Annual mean temperature", "bio01"))`, `r pval(hef(wg_, "Alone: Annual mean temperature", "bio01", "p"))`), as expected because the dry-month criterion depends on temperature. They did not differ in annual precipitation (`r pval(hef(wg_, "Alone: Annual precipitation (log)", "log_bio12", "p"))`), elevation (`r pval(hef(wg_, "Alone: Elevation", "elevation", "p"))`) or tree cover (`r pval(hef(wg_, "Alone: Tree cover", "tree", "p"))`). With temperature, precipitation, tree cover, elevation and productivity in one model, dry months kept their effect (`r num(hef(wg_, "All six", "dry_months"))`, `r pval(hef(wg_, "All six", "dry_months", "p"))`) and temperature lost it (`r pval(hef(wg_, "All six", "bio01", "p"))`).

**Accessible areas and sampling (`s34`).** Hexagons defined by a species' own records make its baseline partly circular, so we drew accessible areas independently: all land within 250 or 500 km of the records, with all land or only pixels holding lycaenid records as background. Within 500 km of all land, the mutualists' places had more dry months (`r num(ntf(500, "all", "dry_months"))`, `r pval(ntf(500, "all", "dry_months", "p"))`), less driest-month rain (`r num(ntf(500, "all", "log_bio14"))`, `r pval(ntf(500, "all", "log_bio14", "p"))`) and more seasonal rainfall (`r num(ntf(500, "all", "bio15"))`, `r pval(ntf(500, "all", "bio15", "p"))`) than accessible, but not more months of water deficit (`r pval(ntf(500, "all", "deficit_months", "p"))`) or a more arid climate (`r pval(ntf(500, "all", "log_aridity", "p"))`). Against the sampled background, dry months remained (`r num(ntf(500, "sampled", "dry_months"))`, `r pval(ntf(500, "sampled", "dry_months", "p"))`) but smaller, and within 250 km of the sampled background nothing was detectable (dry months `r pval(ntf(250, "sampled", "dry_months", "p"))`). The sampled background removes collecting effort, but it also removes real habitat contrasts wherever collectors visit the habitats where lycaenids live, so its weaker result is a conservative bound rather than a refutation.

**Adult flight (`s32`).** If mutualist larvae develop through the dry season inside or beside ant nests, adults might emerge at its end. The months in which adults were recorded, relative to the dry months of their places, showed no detectable difference between obligate mutualists and facultative species (`r fe32[contrast == "mutualist" & analysis == "Given region and lineage" & measure == "dry_flight"]$species` species; all p ≥ `r num(min(fe32[contrast == "mutualist"]$p), 2)`), but the intervals were wide (dry-month flight `r num(fe32[contrast == "mutualist" & analysis == "Given region and lineage" & measure == "dry_flight"]$estimate)` ± `r num(1.96 * fe32[contrast == "mutualist" & analysis == "Given region and lineage" & measure == "dry_flight"]$se)` log odds per SD), and adult records are a weak guide to larval timing in multivoltine tropical species.

## The dry-niche test against all butterfly records {#dryniche}

```{r fig-dryniche, fig.cap = "One estimate per genus (s36): the difference between the obligate mutualists and the facultative species of each genus in their association with dry months, given temperature, relative to the background (log relative intensity per SD), against the records of all butterflies, every recorded pixel weighted equally and all land, with 95% intervals, and the random-effects estimate over genera."}
fig(d36, "plot_dry_niche_genera.png")
```

The comparisons above (`s19`, `s29`, `s34`) did not fully control for the climates available or for where butterflies are recorded. Following the research proposal of 30 October 2026, `s35` and `s36` test three hypotheses: that obligate mutualists occupy seasonally dry environments more than their facultative congeners (H1); that this recurs across independent lineages (H2); and that it reflects the length of the dry season or water stress rather than temperature or the unevenness of rainfall (H3). The null alternative is that availability, sampling or lineage history produce the differences.

**Design.** Each choice was fixed before any model was fitted:

- *Species*: the obligate mutualists and facultative species of the mixed genera (parasites are not part of this test), eligible in an accessible area with at least 20 occupied pixels of 10 arc-minutes there (10 and 30 as sensitivity), and analysed in each area they qualify in.
- *Accessible areas*: each realm on each landmass of the glacial shelf (land above −120 m), so that Borneo, Sumatra and Java join Asia, Tasmania joins Australia and deep-water barriers separate Sulawesi and the Philippines; continental Africa is divided from the Palaearctic in the Sahara; Australia and New Guinea are kept apart (Barve et al. 2011). Alternatives: realms on present-day landmasses, and the study's eight regions.
- *Backgrounds*: the GBIF records of all six butterfly families per pixel, with the focal species' own records removed and counts capped at the 95th percentile of recorded pixels (primary; Phillips et al. 2009; Barber et al. 2022); every recorded pixel weighted equally, which treats detection as saturated; and all land weighted by area, which describes availability regardless of recording. Butterfly records reflect butterfly diversity as well as effort, so the record-weighted models measure occupancy relative to the recorded butterfly assemblage (Botella et al. 2020).
- *Species models*: presence–background point-process models fitted as infinitely weighted logistic regressions (Warton & Shepherd 2010; Fithian & Hastie 2013), with dry months and temperature standardised over the land of the eight regions; standard errors cluster-robust over 2° blocks and never below the model-based ones; penalised smooths for the shapes.
- *Comparisons*: (A) the difference between the mutualists' and the facultative species' coefficients within each genus and area, one estimate per genus, pooled by random-effects meta-analysis, with a hierarchical meta-analysis of the species coefficients as a second estimate, also with a phylogenetic correlation from the genus-grafted Yumnam tree; (B) without a background, whether an occupied pixel belongs to a mutualist or a facultative congener.
- *Outcomes*: strong support if the pooled difference is positive with an interval above zero under the record-weighted background, positive under the other two, positive in at least two thirds of genera and positive without any one genus; lineage-specific support if at least one genus has an interval above zero; otherwise no convincing support.

Three choices depart from the proposal. Records were aggregated to the 10-arc-minute pixels of the climate layers (about 18 km) rather than to 10 km. The cleaned lycaenid records were not supplemented from GBIF, because GBIF records outside the cleaning pipeline would mix two standards; the GBIF counts were used only for the background. Niche-overlap metrics such as Schoener's D were not computed, because they describe how different two niches are, not whether mutualists occupy drier environments.

**Eligibility.** `r nrow(eu36)` species-area units of `r uniqueN(eu36$pool_key)` species qualified, in `r oc36$genera` genera with both strategies in the same area: `r paste(unique(eu36[, paste0("*", genus, "* (", sub(": .*$", "", area), ")")]), collapse = ", ")`. `r el36[in_contrast_20 == FALSE, .N]` species of the mixed genera were not eligible, mostly because their records occupied fewer than 20 pixels or because no congener of the other strategy qualified in the same area (Table S5.16 of the paper). Contrasts are few, and most lie in Australia and Indomalaya.

**Pilot.** On *Arhopala*, *Hypochrysops* and *Ogyris*, every model converged, and the coefficient of dry months given temperature had the sign of the raw difference between the species' dry months and those of its background for `r pct(pil36[background == "record", mean(sign(estimate) == sign(raw_difference))])` of species (the rest differ because temperature is in the model).

**H1, the contrast.** The mutualists' association with dry months, given temperature, exceeded that of their facultative congeners in `r oc36$positive` of `r oc36$genera` genera (Fig. \@ref(fig:fig-dryniche)). The pooled difference was `r num(csf(dm_))` log relative intensity per SD (95% interval `r num(csf(dm_, col = "pooled_low"))` to `r num(csf(dm_, col = "pooled_high"))`, `r pval(csf(dm_, col = "pooled_p"))`) against all butterfly records, `r num(csf(dm_, "cell"))` with recorded pixels weighted equally and `r num(csf(dm_, "uniform"))` against all land. The hierarchical meta-analysis gave `r num(csf(dm_, col = "hierarchical"))` (`r pval(csf(dm_, col = "hierarchical_p"))`), and adding the phylogenetic correlation left it unchanged (`r num(csf(dm_, col = "phylogenetic"))`), because the grafted tree resolves nothing within genera. The outcome under the rules set in advance: **`r tolower(oc36$outcome)`**.

**H2, repeatability.** The positive genera were `r paste0("*", gen36[difference > 0]$genus, "*", collapse = ", ")`; the negative ones `r paste0("*", gen36[difference <= 0]$genus, "*", collapse = ", ")`, each with few species. No genus differed clearly on its own: the intervals of single genera are wide because most contrasts rest on one to four species per strategy. Leaving out any one genus kept the pooled difference between `r num(min(logo36$pooled))` and `r num(max(logo36$pooled))` (without *Arhopala* `r num(logo36[setting == "Without Arhopala"]$pooled)`), so no single lineage carries the direction; the interval was above zero only `r if (any(logo36$pooled_low > 0)) paste0("without ", paste0("*", sub("^Without ", "", logo36[pooled_low > 0]$setting), "*", collapse = " or "), ", which goes the other way") else "in none of these sets"`. The direction recurs across lineages in Australia, Indomalaya and Africa; its size is not established.

**H3, what kind of dryness.** Given temperature, the pooled differences were:

- dry months `r num(mp(dm_))` (`r pval(mp(dm_, "pooled_p"))`);
- climatic water deficit `r num(mp("Climatic water deficit, given temperature"))` (`r pval(mp("Climatic water deficit, given temperature", "pooled_p"))`);
- less driest-month rain `r num(mp("Less driest-month rain, given temperature"))` (`r pval(mp("Less driest-month rain, given temperature", "pooled_p"))`);
- months below 50 mm, a dry-season length that does not depend on temperature, `r num(mp("Months below 50 mm, given temperature"))` (`r pval(mp("Months below 50 mm, given temperature", "pooled_p"))`);
- water-deficit months `r num(mp("Water-deficit months, given temperature"))` (`r pval(mp("Water-deficit months, given temperature", "pooled_p"))`) and precipitation seasonality `r num(mp("Precipitation seasonality, given temperature"))` (`r pval(mp("Precipitation seasonality, given temperature", "pooled_p"))`).

Without temperature, dry months gave `r num(mp("Dry months alone"))` (`r num(mp("Dry months alone", "pooled_low"))` to `r num(mp("Dry months alone", "pooled_high"))`), the one interval above zero, and temperature alone `r num(mp("Temperature alone"))` (`r pval(mp("Temperature alone", "pooled_p"))`; hierarchical `r pval(mp("Temperature alone", "hierarchical_p"))`). The mutualists' places are thus both drier and warmer than their congeners' relative to the background, and the dry-month definition itself depends on temperature (P < 2T). These data do not separate a dry-season signal from a warmth signal. The earlier reading, seasonal drought rather than aridity (`s34`), also weakens: the climatic water deficit, which integrates evaporative demand over the year, gave a difference as large as dry months.

**Robustness.** With the record-weighted background, the pooled difference ranged over `r num(rng36("Threshold")[1])`–`r num(rng36("Threshold")[2])` for thresholds of 10 and 30 pixels, `r num(rng36("Accessible area")[1])`–`r num(rng36("Accessible area")[2])` for the other accessible areas, `r num(csf("30 arc-minutes", grp = "Resolution"))` at 30 arc-minutes, `r num(csf("Species-specific evidence only", grp = "Species"))` with species-specific evidence only, and `r num(csf("Overlapping a congener of the other strategy", grp = "Species"))` for species whose records overlap a congener of the other strategy. All are positive, and none has an interval above zero.

**Without a background.** Pixels occupied by mutualists had more dry months than those of their facultative congeners in the same genus and area (`r num(dcf("All genera"))` log odds per SD, cluster-robust `r pval(dcf("All genera", "p_value"))`; `r num(min(dc36[grepl("^Without", setting)]$estimate))` to `r num(max(dc36[grepl("^Without", setting)]$estimate))` leaving out each genus), and more months below 50 mm (`r num(dcf("All genera: months below 50 mm"))`, `r pval(dcf("All genera: months below 50 mm", "p_value"))`). This comparison needs no background but assumes that mutualists and facultative congeners were recorded in the same way.

**Prediction.** In spatially blocked cross-validation, the median AUC of held-out 5° blocks was `r num(median(cv36$temperature, na.rm = TRUE))` with temperature alone and `r num(median(cv36$primary, na.rm = TRUE))` with dry months added; dry months improved the prediction for `r cv36[is.finite(gain), sum(gain > 0)]` of `r cv36[is.finite(gain), .N]` species (mutualists `r cv36[is.finite(gain) & strategy == "m", sum(gain > 0)]` of `r cv36[is.finite(gain) & strategy == "m", .N]`).

### Version 2 {-}

```{r fig-dryniche-v2, fig.cap = "Version 2 (s37): one estimate per origin of obligate mutualism, the difference between its mutualists and their facultative relatives in the association with dry months relative to the background, under three backgrounds, and the joint model (model-based interval; thin line: bootstrap over origins)."}
fig(d37, "plot_dry_niche_origins.png")
```

Version 1 could detect only differences of about `r num((qnorm(0.975) + qnorm(0.8)) * csf(dm_, col = "pooled_se"), 1)` per SD with 80% power, so after it was run we declared a second version in writing (`writing/dry_niche_v2_plan.md`) before fitting it (`s37`). It changed four things: dry months alone became the primary measure (H1 concerns dry-season duration; temperature serves H3) — **a choice made after seeing version 1, in which dry months alone was the one measure whose interval excluded zero**; occurrences were supplemented with each species' own GBIF records within 100 km of its cleaned records; each origin of obligate mutualism formed one contrast, using the nearest facultative clade on the tree of genera, within a subfamily, when a genus had no eligible facultative species; and all species entered one point-process model with random slopes of species and origins.

**What changed in the data.** Supplementation added `r format(read(d37, "presences.csv")[source == "GBIF", .N], big.mark = ",")` occupied pixels. The origin rule added one contrast, `r unique(ct37[grepl(" vs ", contrast)]$contrast)`, with `r ct37[grepl(" vs ", contrast) & strategy == "m", .N]` mutualists from several South African Aphnaeinae genera against `r ct37[grepl(" vs ", contrast) & strategy == "f", .N]` facultative species; the Australian candidates (*Jalmenus*, *Pseudalmenus*) found no eligible facultative species outside other contrasts before the clade search left their subfamily on the tree of genera. Version 2 thus has `r jf(col = "units")` species-area units in `r jf(col = "origins")` origins.

**Result.** The joint estimate for dry months was `r num(jf())` (model-based 95% interval `r num(jf(col = "low"))` to `r num(jf(col = "high"))`, `r pval(jf(col = "p"))`; cluster bootstrap over origins `r num(oc37$bootstrap_low)` to `r num(oc37$bootstrap_high)`, with `r pct(mean(read(d37, "bootstrap.csv")$estimate > 0, na.rm = TRUE))` of resamples positive), `r num(jf(bg_ = "cell"))` with recorded pixels weighted equally and `r num(jf(bg_ = "uniform"))` against all land. Leaving out each origin gave `r num(oc37$loo_min)` to `r num(oc37$loo_max)` (lowest without *`r oc37$loo_min_without`*). The two-stage estimate was `r num(tsf())` (`r num(tsf(col = "pooled_low"))` to `r num(tsf(col = "pooled_high"))`), positive in `r oc37$positive` of `r oc37$origins` origins; the new Aphnaeinae contrast was `r num(to37[step == v2_ & model == "primary" & background == "record" & grepl("Aloeides", origin)]$difference)`. Under the rules declared in advance: **`r tolower(oc37$outcome)`**.

**Step by step.** The joint model on version 1's data gave `r num(jf(st = "Version 1 data (within genera, cleaned records)"))` (`r pval(jf(st = "Version 1 data (within genera, cleaned records)", col = "p"))`); adding supplementation lowered it to `r num(jf(st = "Adding GBIF supplementation"))` (`r pval(jf(st = "Adding GBIF supplementation", col = "p"))`), mainly because the extra pixels moved *Ogyris* and *Plebejus* towards zero or below; adding the origin contrasts gave `r num(jf())`. The changes that added data thus weakened the estimate; the joint model, which uses the data more efficiently, narrowed the interval.

**H3 in version 2.** Given temperature, the joint estimate was `r num(jf("given_temperature"))` (`r pval(jf("given_temperature", col = "p"))`); months below 50 mm given temperature `r num(jf("dry50"))` (`r pval(jf("dry50", col = "p"))`); temperature alone `r num(jf("temperature"))` (`r pval(jf("temperature", col = "p"))`). Dryness and warmth remain inseparable here.

**Reading.** The direction is consistent: across backgrounds, accessible areas, thresholds, resolutions, evidence, both versions and every leave-one-out set, mutualists lean towards drier places than their facultative relatives. But the contrast holds in only about half of the independent origins, its size depends on which species are included, its bootstrap interval includes zero, and it cannot be separated from warmth. Version 2 did not change the conclusion of version 1; it narrowed the estimate to a modest positive difference that the data cannot establish. Phase 3 of the proposal (larval phenology, nest use, host plants and attendance) was conditional on consistent differentiation; by the rules set in advance it is not triggered, but the direction makes it worth doing for the genera with the largest positive contrasts (`r paste0("*", gen36[order(-difference)][difference > 0]$genus, "*", collapse = ", ")`).

## Ants {#ants}

**Richness and partner genera (`s21`).** Given region and lineage, the estimated ant species richness of a species' records had no detectable effect on obligacy (`r num(ar("obligate", "region and lineage"))` log odds per SD, 95% interval `r num(ar("obligate", "region and lineage") - 1.96 * ar("obligate", "region and lineage", "se"))` to `r num(ar("obligate", "region and lineage") + 1.96 * ar("obligate", "region and lineage", "se"))`). Of the `r obl_partner` obligate species with recorded partners, `r obl_cc` were recorded with *Crematogaster* or *Camponotus*. Both genera occur in the Cape, southern Australia, the Mediterranean Basin and California, and are richest in the Basin (`r av("Crematogaster", "Mediterranean Basin")` *Crematogaster* and `r av("Camponotus", "Mediterranean Basin")` *Camponotus* species, against `r av("Crematogaster", "Cape")` and `r av("Camponotus", "Cape")` in the Cape), where `r av("Crematogaster", "Mediterranean Basin", "f")` and `r av("Camponotus", "Mediterranean Basin", "f")` facultative lycaenids were recorded with them. The other partner genera of southern obligate species were mostly regional, such as *Iridomyrmex* and *Anonychomyrma* in Australia and *Anoplolepis* in southern Africa.

**Local communities (`s27`).** In the `r format(nrow(loc27), big.mark = ",")` sampled communities of the Global Ant Database, the two partner genera made up a median `r pct(rc("Southern Africa", "partner_species"))` of the ant species of a locality in southern Africa and `r pct(rc("Australia", "partner_species"))` in Australia, against `r pct(rc("Palearctic", "partner_species"))` in the Palaearctic and `r pct(rc("Nearctic", "partner_species"))` in the Nearctic. Communities were more dominated by their most abundant species in southern Africa and Australia (`r pct(rc("Southern Africa", "dominance"))` and `r pct(rc("Australia", "dominance"))` of individuals) than in the Palaearctic and Nearctic (`r pct(rc("Palearctic", "dominance"))` and `r pct(rc("Nearctic", "dominance"))`), but nearly as much in Indomalaya and New Guinea (`r pct(rc("Indomalayan", "dominance"))` and `r pct(rc("New Guinea and islands", "dominance"))`). Adjusted for the species and individuals sampled, only Australia remained more dominated than the Palaearctic (`r num(da27[region == "Australia"]$estimate)` on the logit scale, `r pval(da27[region == "Australia"]$p)`). Dominance was computed only where individuals were counted (`r format(loc27[is.finite(dominance), .N], big.mark = ",")` localities; none of the `r rc("Cape", "localities")` localities of the Cape). The relationship with obligacy reversed with scale. Across hexagons without region, more dominated communities went with weakly more obligate lycaenids (`r num(hm27[measure == "dominance" & given_region == FALSE]$estimate)` log odds per SD, `r pval(hm27[measure == "dominance" & given_region == FALSE]$p)`). Within regions, they went with fewer (`r num(hm27[measure == "dominance" & given_region == TRUE]$estimate)`, `r pval(hm27[measure == "dominance" & given_region == TRUE]$p)`; `r hm27[measure == "dominance" & given_region == TRUE]$hexagons` hexagons).

**Colony traits (`s30`).** Colony size (workers in mature colonies; Bell-Roberts et al. 2024) was available for `r pa30[is.finite(colony_size), .N]` of the `r nrow(pa30)` partner species. Within ant genera, the species recorded with obligate lycaenids had colonies about `r num(10^at30[grepl("^log10 colony size, obligate partners vs facultative only .genus RE", test)]$estimate, 1)` times as large as those recorded only with facultative ones (`r pval(at30[grepl("^log10 colony size, obligate partners vs facultative only .genus RE", test)]$p)`); they were not more often polygynous or supercolonial. Across `r gt30[grepl("Spearman", test)]$genera` partner genera, median colony size was unrelated to the obligate share of the genus's lycaenid partners (Spearman `r num(gt30[grepl("Spearman", test)]$estimate)`, `r pval(gt30[grepl("Spearman", test)]$p)`). Among lycaenid species, those whose partners had larger colonies (species values, otherwise genus medians) were more often obligate mutualists, given region and lineage (`r num(ltf("mutualist", "partner_cs", "region and lineage"))` log odds per SD, `r pval(ltf("mutualist", "partner_cs", "region and lineage", "p"))`; `r ltf("mutualist", "partner_cs", "region and lineage", "species")` species). With species values only, the estimate was larger but uncertain (`r num(lsp("estimate"))`, `r pval(lsp("p"))`; `r lsp("species")` species, `r lsp("events")` mutualists). The regions differ: the median partner colony of Australia's obligate lycaenids had about `r format(round(rps("Australia", "obligate"), -2), big.mark = ",")` workers against `r format(round(rps("Australia", "facultative"), -2), big.mark = ",")` for its facultative species, whereas in southern Africa the obligate species' partners had about `r format(round(rps("Southern Africa", "obligate"), -2), big.mark = ",")` against `r format(round(rps("Southern Africa", "facultative"), -2), big.mark = ",")`, and in the Palaearctic, where many obligate species are parasites of *Myrmica*, about `r format(round(rps("Palearctic", "obligate"), -2), big.mark = ",")` against `r format(round(rps("Palearctic", "facultative"), -2), big.mark = ",")`.

## History of obligacy {#history}

```{r fig-history, fig.cap = "History of obligacy (s17). (A) The classified species on the genus-grafted, dated tree of Yumnam & Kodandaramaiah (2025), with their strategy (inner ring) and hemisphere (outer ring). (B) Origins of obligacy per region on the tree of genera, the published trees pruned to their matched species, and the genus-grafted species tree."}
fig(d17, "figure_history.png")
```

**Origins (`s09`, `s10`, `s14`).** Obligacy arose repeatedly, but the number of origins in each region depends on the tree. On the tree of genera, which does not depend on placements within genera, it arose `r og_med("Southern Africa")` times in southern Africa (`r og_gen("Southern Africa")` obligate genera) and `r og_med("Australia")` times in Australia (`r og_gen("Australia")` genera). The species trees added shallow origins within genera, mainly in Australia (`r os("Australia", "origins_median")`) and Indomalaya (`r os("Indomalayan", "origins_median")`), stable over 20 random resolutions of the grafted polytomies. Without grafting, obligacy arose `r omv("yumnam_2025", "Australia")` times in Australia on the pruned Yumnam tree, but southern Africa's obligate species are poorly represented there (`r omv("yumnam_2025", "Southern Africa", "obligate")` of `r lin_n("Southern Africa", "m") + lin_n("Southern Africa", "p")`). Whether gains and losses depend on hemisphere depended on the tree (Yumnam `r pval(ptest[tree == "yumnam_2025"]$p)`; Schär `r pval(ptest[tree == "schar_2018"]$p)`, which has Grafen branch lengths).

**Rates per unit of lineage history (`s25`).** A region with more lineage history offers more opportunities for obligacy to arise, so we divided the gains in each region group by the time its lineages spent non-obligate. Southern Africa and Australia gained obligacy `r num(rr25(ts, "ratio_median"), 1)` times as often as elsewhere on the pruned Yumnam tree (95% range over maps `r num(rr25(ts, "ratio_low"), 1)`–`r num(rr25(ts, "ratio_high"), 1)`), `r num(rr25(tg, "ratio_median"), 1)` times on the tree of genera, and `r num(rr25(tk, "ratio_median"), 1)` times on the tree of genera from Kawahara et al. (2023). Against gains placed at random along the non-obligate history (binomial placement by exposure), one-sided p ranged from `r num(min(r25$p_null))` to `r num(max(r25$p_null))`. The southern origins were older (median `r num(median(ga25[tree == tg & group == "South"]$age), 0)` Myr on the tree of genera) than those of the Holarctic and the Americas (`r num(median(ga25[tree == tg & group == "Holarctic and Americas"]$age), 0)` Myr). Net diversification rates of genera were estimated earlier (`s10`) but are not used, because they cannot separate speciation from extinction (Rabosky & Benson 2021).

# From patterns to processes: the sixth review {#processes}

The sixth external review asked for the next stage to aim at processes, not more patterns, with feasibility checked before larger models. The assessment, the conceptual model, the ranked roadmap with its decision rules, and the results are in `writing/research_roadmap.md`; this section reports the analyses (`s38`–`s44`). All were designed after the earlier results were known, so they are sequential; their variables, settings and outcome rules were fixed before each was run.

**Conceptual model.** Three interacting processes: (A) assembly of regional species pools (dispersal, diversification, geographical restriction); (B) environmental filtering of where the species of those lineages occur; (C) the interaction strategy itself, which may change the niche (C → B) and spread (C → A) of a lineage. Environment may also shape where obligacy evolves. Our data test A → strategy mix (shared climates, decomposition), B (within-region gradients, matched comparisons) and C → A (confinement) as patterns or associations; none of the pathways reaches a supported mechanism.

**Three hypotheses for the dry-season signal**, each with one variable fixed in advance: H1 warmth (annual mean temperature); H2 dry-season duration independent of temperature (the longest run of months below 50 mm); H3 water stress (the annual climatic water deficit).

## Can drought be told apart from warmth? {-}

```{r fig-identifiability, fig.cap = "Environmental space of each contrast (s38): annual mean temperature against the run of months below 50 mm, for the butterfly records of the accessible area (grey), the occupied pixels of mutualists (orange) and facultative relatives (blue), and the common temperature support (dashed)."}
fig(d38, "plot_environment_space_run.png")
```

Yes, with temperature-independent measures. Within the `r uniqueN(id38$contrast)` contrasts, the run of months below 50 mm correlated with temperature at r = `r num(min(id38[variable == "dry_run50"]$cor_occupied))` to `r num(max(id38[variable == "dry_run50"]$cor_occupied))` among the occupied pixels, and the run and the water deficit kept `r pct(min(id38$sd_ratio))`–`r pct(max(id38$sd_ratio))` of their variation within 1 °C temperature bins. Every contrast passed the identifiability rule. The confounding of drought with warmth in `s36`–`s37` came from the Gaussen definition of dry months (precipitation in mm below twice the temperature), which builds temperature in. One caveat: in *Hypochrysops*, only `r pct(id38[contrast == "Hypochrysops (Australia)" & variable == "dry_run50"]$share_m_in_support)` of the mutualists' pixels lie within the temperature range shared with the facultative species.

## What the GBIF supplementation did, and how many origins there are {-}

Of the `r format(nrow(sp39), big.mark = ",")` pixels added from GBIF in `s37`, `r format(sp39[reason != "No record in the parent download", .N], big.mark = ",")` held records that the parent cleaning had removed, mostly by its basic coordinate, basis and duplicate filters. The pooled dry-month difference fell from `r num(sd39$pooled[1])` with cleaned records to `r num(sd39$pooled[2])` when the same species were re-estimated with supplemented records, and to `r num(sd39$pooled[3])` when the `r sd39$units[3] - sd39$units[2]` species-area units that became eligible only through supplementation were added. The added records were ordinary (mostly iNaturalist research-grade observations, national recording schemes and museum specimens, with routine GBIF flags), so the change is a composition effect: the estimate depends on which species are included. Cleaned records are primary from here on.

The ten contrasts form nine origins, but only `r og39[mutualists >= 2 & facultative >= 2, .N]` have at least two species of each strategy, and the largest pairs `r og39[which.max(mutualists)]$mutualists` mutualists with `r og39[which.max(mutualists)]$facultative` facultative species. On the matched species tree, mutualists form several clades within *Hypochrysops*, *Ogyris*, *Cigaritis* and the Aphnaeinae contrast, but these share the same few facultative relatives, so the real replication remains about nine weakly balanced contrasts.

## Which data would help? {-}

```{r fig-power, fig.cap = "Power simulation (s40): power to detect a mutualist-minus-facultative difference of 0.5 or 0.8 log relative intensity per SD, and the median width of the 95% interval, under scenarios of added data."}
fig(d40, "plot_power.png")
```
